title: Valid Sudoku
corePattern: Hash Set Validation with Partitioned Constraints (Row / Column / Box Direct Addressing)
interviewTips: Ask if board is always 9x9 with only '1'-'9' and '.' - you only check current validity, not solvability.
Trade-off: three-pass boolean arrays are clearest to explain; single-pass bitmask with 27 integers is fastest and most space-efficient.
Edge-case tip: always skip '.'; box index is (i/3)*3 + j/3 and digit index is c - '1'; test duplicate in same box but different rows and columns.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Three-Pass Validation with Hash Sets
approaches.intuition: Check Sudoku rules separately: every row must have no duplicates, every column must have no duplicates, every 3x3 box must have no duplicates. Use a fresh set for each unit and fail fast on repeat.
approaches.theory: A valid board means 27 independent units (9 rows + 9 columns + 9 boxes) each contain distinct digits ignoring '.'. Validating each unit with a hash set is correct because duplicates are exactly set collisions. Three passes visit each cell three times: 9 rows x 9 cells + 9 cols x 9 cells + 9 boxes x 9 cells = 243 operations, which is constant for 9x9 and O(N^2) for general NxN.

timeComplexity.explanation: Fixed 9x9 board visits 81 cells three times = 243 operations. In general for NxN board it is O(N^2).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only one set or boolean array of size up to 9 per unit, reused across units.

dryRunExample.input: board[0][0]='5', board[0][1]='3', board[0][2]='.', board[1][0]='6' ... with duplicate '8' in column
steps: Row pass: rows 0-8 have no internal duplicates, continue.
Column pass: column 2 finds '8' at row 1 and again at row 2 -> collision.
Return false immediately without checking boxes.

edgeCases: Duplicate in row but different boxes -> false
Duplicate in column but different boxes -> false
Duplicate in 3x3 box but different rows and columns -> false

approaches.name: Approach 2: Single Pass with Bitmask Direct Addressing
approaches.intuition: Track row, column, and box constraints together in one scan. Each digit 1-9 maps to one bit; three integer arrays rows[9], cols[9], boxes[9] record which digits have been seen. Box index is (i/3)*3 + j/3.
approaches.theory: Digits are limited to 9 values, so a 9-bit integer is a perfect hash set with O(1) insert and lookup via bitwise AND/OR. For cell (i,j) with bit = 1 << (c-'1') and b = (i/3)*3 + j/3, validity requires bit not already present in rows[i], cols[j], boxes[b]. If present, board is invalid; otherwise set the bit. Single traversal maintains invariant that masks exactly represent seen digits so far.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single scan of 81 cells with O(1) bit operations per cell. Generally O(N^2) for NxN board.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Three arrays of 9 integers (27 ints) for row/col/box masks, independent of board content.

dryRunExample.input: board with valid prefix, cell (0,2)='8', cell (1,2)='8' in same box and column
steps: Process (0,2): bit=1<<7, b=1, rows[0], cols[2], boxes[1] do not have bit -> set them.
Process (1,2): bit=1<<7, b=1, cols[2] already has bit and boxes[1] already has bit -> collision.

edgeCases: Sparse board with single digit -> true
Same digit in different boxes, rows, cols is allowed -> true
Full valid board with no '.' -> true if all constraints hold
